title: HSBC, ICICI Lead GIFT City's $19.3 Billion NRI Lending Boom
excerpt: Moneycontrol reported NRI-linked lending at $19.3 billion as banks use offshore GIFT City units to offer leveraged FCNR-B deposits, riding the RBI's hedging-cost subsidies.
body:
• Moneycontrol reported that HSBC and ICICI Bank are leading an NRI lending boom out of GIFT City, with lending linked to non-resident clients running at $19.3 billion.
  • HSBC's GIFT City branch is offering NRI clients leverage of up to 19 times their FCNR-B placements; SBI is offering up to nine times.
  • Overall FCNR-B balances across Indian banks nearly doubled from $32.56 billion on June 5 to $60.55 billion by July 30 after the RBI began absorbing hedging costs.
  • Reuters reported the RBI mobilised $136.4 billion between June 5 and August 31, including $127 billion from non-resident deposits.

India's Gujarat International Finance Tec-City is emerging as the offshore engine of a non-resident lending boom. Moneycontrol reported that HSBC and ICICI Bank are leading the charge, with NRI-linked lending out of GIFT City running at $19.3 billion, as banks use their international financial services centre units to court overseas Indians with leveraged deposit products.

The boom sits atop the Reserve Bank of India's June 5 measures to pull in dollar liquidity: the central bank offered to bear the full hedging cost for banks raising fresh foreign currency non-resident (FCNR-B) deposits with three-to-five-year tenors, and exempted those deposits from cash reserve ratio and statutory liquidity ratio requirements. According to Reuters, the RBI received $136.4 billion under the schemes between June 5 and August 31 — including a much higher-than-expected $127 billion from non-resident deposits alone.

Leverage is the magnet

What makes GIFT City the centre of gravity is leverage. HSBC's GIFT City branch offers non-resident Indian clients leverage of up to 19 times their FCNR-B placements, while State Bank of India offers up to nine times, according to Outlook Business. Banks believe their GIFT City units, operating under offshore banking rules, function like foreign banks and should be permitted to fund these deposits through lending — Reuters reported in June that lenders were seeking the RBI's explicit approval for the practice.

The arithmetic is compelling for depositors. With the RBI subsidising hedging costs, banks can offer dollar-deposit rates well above what NRIs earn abroad — Federal Bank quotes around 7–7.5 per cent on fresh FCNR-B deposits, while larger banks quote roughly 6 per cent — and leveraged placements magnify the return further.

ICICI's product push

ICICI Bank, one of the leaders named in Moneycontrol's reporting, has been building out its GIFT City NRI shelf. Its branch there offers Loan Against Deposits, which lets NRI customers take a foreign-currency loan of up to 95 per cent of their deposit value — including rupee NRE fixed deposits — without prematurely breaking the deposit, alongside dollar bonds from a roster of more than 50 issuers.

"Foreign currency bonds are one of the preferred investment options amongst NRI clients. We want to provide our customers with the ease of banking digitally, driving a seamless journey and a hassle-free experience."

— Sriram H. Iyer, Head of International Banking Group, ICICI Bank

Government data cited by Outlook Business shows the four largest public-sector lenders — SBI, Bank of Baroda, Canara Bank and Punjab National Bank — held a combined FCNR-B portfolio of nearly $21 billion as of July 30, against about $18.5 billion for the four largest private banks. SBI alone held roughly $6 billion and set a target of at least $10 billion by end-September.

How big the wave gets

Nomura estimated the scheme could attract $55 billion in total, and SBI's economists have projected FCNR-B collections of $65–70 billion with combined inflows across all channels reaching $80–85 billion. The special FCNR-B window remains open until September 30, and the external commercial borrowing and overseas foreign currency borrowing windows run to December 31.

There are caveats. Analysts warn that leveraged deposit schemes carry rollover risk: the flows that boost reserves today must be refinanced or repaid when the deposits mature. RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra has dismissed concerns about recycling of existing deposits as insignificant, but economists at HDFC Bank and IDFC First Bank have noted timing lags in banks swapping deposits with the RBI and questioned how much of the headline figure represents genuinely new money.

What it means for NRIs

For overseas Indians, the practical takeaway is timing. The concessional-hedging window closes September 30, and the rate advantage on FCNR-B deposits is a policy artifact, not a permanent feature of the market. Gulf-based investors have been the strongest source of demand so far. US-based investors should note that interest earned remains subject to US personal income tax — the headline rate is not the take-home rate.
image_caption: The ICICI Bank branch at K.G. Marg in New Delhi. ICICI is among the lenders financing GIFT City's fast-growing NRI loan book, where a new deposit scheme is drawing heavy dollar inflows from overseas Indians.
nri_angle: NRIs in the Gulf and US are the direct beneficiaries: leveraged FCNR-B deposits through GIFT City offer dollar yields well above Western rates, but the September 30 window and rollover risk demand attention.
author: Diaspora Desk
